## Structure and components

- [statement] AWS describes long-running shadow variants as a way to validate candidate serving-stack components before promoting them to production. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-16) — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/model-shadow-deployment.html

## How it works

- [statement] Google identifies training-serving pipeline discrepancies, data changes and model feedback loops as causes of training-serving skew. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-16) — https://developers.google.com/machine-learning/guides/rules-of-ml
- [statement] Google frames model freshness as a system-specific requirement and notes it can change when features are added or removed. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-16) — https://developers.google.com/machine-learning/guides/rules-of-ml

## Comparisons and alternatives

- [statement] Google recommends comparing training versus holdout, holdout versus next-day, and next-day versus live performance when diagnosing skew. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-16) — https://developers.google.com/machine-learning/guides/rules-of-ml

## Facts and statements

- [statement] Google recommends recording the actual features used at serving time and reusing those logged features for training. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-16) — https://developers.google.com/machine-learning/guides/rules-of-ml
- [statement] Google notes that mutable joined feature tables can make a prediction differ between training and serving. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-16) — https://developers.google.com/machine-learning/guides/rules-of-ml
- [statement] Google recommends checking held-out performance before exporting a model, and withholding export if concerns remain about the data. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-16) — https://developers.google.com/machine-learning/guides/rules-of-ml
